title: Complementing Self-Consistency with Cross-Model Disagreement for Uncertainty Quantification
claim: Self-consistency looks confident when models agree internally but err, whereas cross-model disagreement exposes the failure and improves uncertainty ranking.
layout: 2 panels, left example then right heatmap and bar chart, brace linking responses
description: The left panel shows a factual question in a speech bubble: who won the Oceanography Society's Jerlov Award in 2018, with the target answer Annick Bricaud shown in green. Two rounded boxes, a blue GPT-4o and a green Claude 3.7 Sonnet, each sit above three sampled answers in red monospace text. GPT-4o repeatedly answers Raymond C. Smith and Claude repeatedly answers Kenneth J. Voss. Each set is marked with a red X. Below, the text says self-consistency is high within each model. A curly brace joins the two answer sets and leads to the text 'Inter-model disagreement ⇒ EU: high'. The right panel has a red-blue heatmap of AUROC for Aleatoric, Total and Epistemic uncertainty, with one row per model. A small blue bar chart of average accuracy sits beside it.
caption: (a) Two models confidently produce distinct, incorrect answers to a factual question, which results in low intra-model variability (AU) but high semantic disagreement across models (EU). (b) Total uncertainty (TU = AU + EU) effectively improves uncertainty calibration with correcness in terms of AUROC on SimpleQA.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce confident yet incorrect responses, and uncertainty quantification is one potential solution to more robust usage. Recent works routinely rely on self-consistency to estimate aleatoric uncertainty (AU), yet this proxy collapses when models are overconfident and produce the same incorrect answer across samples. We analyze this regime and show that cross-model semantic disagreement is higher on incorrect answers precisely when AU is low. Motivated by this, we introduce an epistemic uncertainty (EU) term that operates in the black-box access setting: EU uses only generated text from a small, scale-matched ensemble and is computed as the gap between inter-model and intra-model sequence-semantic similarity. We then define total uncertainty (TU) as the sum of AU and EU. In a comprehensive study across five 7-9B instruction-tuned models and ten long-form tasks, TU improves ranking calibration and selective abstention relative to AU, and EU reliably flags confident failures where AU is low. We further characterize when EU is most useful via agreement and complementarity diagnostics.
